extracted.intended_audience: students and novice academic writers (particularly in mathematics) seeking composition exercises and editorial guidance
extracted.subtask_description: A handout and lecture notes giving composition exercises and practical editorial/style guidance aimed at improving clarity, voice, structure, and technical writing habits (with many exercises to practice specific skills). Geared especially toward mathematicians but generally applicable to academic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphatic positions
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the emphatic positions? The front of the sentence and the back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary where emphasis falls in sentences; try writing sentences with different emphases to discover effects ("The middle of a sentence is sort of a slum.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Write nonsense (coherent nonsense with correct glue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a completely unrelated stream of thoughts with the correct glue: Words like 'thus,' 'therefore,' and 'as we can see.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a paragraph of coherent, tightly structured nonsense (made-up words not allowed). Mary‑Claire recommends this as a fun exercise (possibly after a couple of drinks) to learn phrasing and connective usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual labor — copying by hand and other media
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy out a passage of your own writing or someone else's with a pen; with a pencil; with a crayon; with left and right hand; with a manual typewriter; with a word-processor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual copying slows the brain to allow close reading and attention to form. Copying from a wide variety of sources (liked/disliked, hard/easy, old/recent, hurried/overwritten) yields different insights; typing vs longhand connects different hand/brain processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying for close reading (exploratory vs analytic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy a passage from something you like; from something you dislike; from something difficult to read; from something laughably easy; from someone you'd like to imitate; from someone completely unlike you; old and recent texts; scrawled or overwritten samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first copying exercise is exploratory; the broader set yields inexhaustible information about style, diction, and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen sounds — transcription practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribe five minutes of radio news, public lecture, television dialog, or ordinary conversation from a tape recorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcription trains ear for cadence and phrasing; listening and transcribing helps detect natural speech rhythms versus written diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen sounds — reading aloud and listening
rubrics_metrics.description: Read aloud a page of your own writing; ask a friend or stranger to read it aloud; learn to mutter what you're writing as you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing your writing aloud checks cadence and tone and is an efficient way to spot problems in phrasing and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks on paper — iterative drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that writing is 'the most forgiving medium known to man.' We can work on it until we get it right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ability to revise as a tool: write, look, revise iteratively. Quoted aphorism: 'How do I know what I mean till I see what I say?' (E. M. Forster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance, voice, and tone — exaggeration therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrow techniques from speech therapists: exaggerate defects until you understand what characterizes them (e.g., if told you are 'breezy,' write something truly off the wall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include changing stance, taking both sides, hyperbolizing, euphemizing, obfuscating, pontificating, vacillating, strengthening/vitiating, and changing tone to discover and control voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance exercises — change audience/context
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a text for different audiences: a textbook explanation as a personal letter to a nephew, as a report to an examining psychiatrist, as a People magazine piece, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapting to different stances sharpens awareness of register, audience assumptions, and necessary detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument exercises — take both sides and vacillate
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a vigorous, closely reasoned argument for some small proposal and then write an equally vigorous argument against it; inject doubts and hesitations into argumentative passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises develop the ability to see and present opposing reasoning and to modulate rhetorical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone modulation (hyperbolize, euphemize, obfuscate, pontificate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite passages to change register: make them sarcastic/non-sarcastic, vivid/plain, euphemistic/plain, obscure/clear, or pompous/modest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicing these transformations trains control over diction, politeness strategies, and rhetorical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation — expand and contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a paragraph describing a small daily event; expand it to five pages; then reduce it back to a paragraph and compare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This measures compression skills and sensitivity to what details are essential vs superfluous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation — rethink & sensualize
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe an event by appearance only, or by sounds only; describe objects by texture, color, smell, taste, touch; choose an object and describe it as a sensory experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises sharpen perception and specificity in descriptive writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same as / different from — compare and analogize
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose two unlike things and build a simile capturing a point of similarity; invent analogies to explain complex systems to varied audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy construction teaches how to map unfamiliar ideas to familiar domains and clarifies distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate (lexical distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose several near-synonyms and write short dictionary-like entries distinguishing them; explain how words differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps sharpen precise word choice and recognition of subtle semantic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention — chance-combination prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick random words from a dictionary and force them into sentences; categorize random nouns and explain the scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises train associative thinking and methods for generating ideas from constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion / verse-writing to strengthen prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Render prose into verse forms (couplets, villanelle, sonnets, ballads), verify meter changes, or write new sonnets daily (and discard them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verse-writing is 'to other composition exercises what lifting hundred-pound weights is to touching your toes' — it builds control of cadence, stress, and economy of language; honor conventional rhyme and stress to gain benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion — metric transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explode or contract a line's meter (e.g., tetrameter to pentameter) without altering meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimenting with meter forces you to think about stress and rhythm in phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precis — reduction and abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a passage and reduce word count by given percentages (e.g., 5%, 25%, 50%) without changing meaning; describe an article or book in no more than ten sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn where structure must change to compress; expect to dispense with some details but not to alter meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly real — reordering and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Flip a paragraph so the last sentence becomes first; rewrite to enforce a leisurely pace or to make it quick and light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises test coherence under syntactic reordering and teach control over narrative pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly real — crunch (avoid adjectives/adverbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a 1000-word description without adjectives or adverbs, or write a 100-word concrete description without adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraining descriptive language forces reliance on nouns and verbs, sharpening concreteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly real — unpack metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a metaphorical passage and rewrite it as prose of flat-footed comparisons and explicit statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies the literal content behind figurative language and tests clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly real — define and exemplify
rubrics_metrics.description: Write dictionary definitions for common words and compare to existing dictionary entries; give multiple instances of an abstract noun and impose an order on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition exercises test precision and ability to prioritize examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly real — instruct and explain
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a simple recipe or instruction so it's suitable for a complete novice; write instructions that let someone draw or build a complicated object without naming parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests ability to decompose tasks and communicate procedural knowledge clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ben Franklin's exercise (reconstruction from hints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce a 3–4 page passage to one- or two-word hints on separate slips, jumble them, leave them for weeks, then reconstruct the passage and compare to original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests memory of structure and relative importance of content; reveals what features of text are most memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push (timed freewriting without repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write sentences at a deliberate pace for five minutes without repeating yourself, without writing nonsense, and without stopping; increase duration gradually (aim for 20 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builds fluency and sustained production under constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary replacement and thesaurus work
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a five-page passage and replace at least three words in every sentence with approximately synonymous words; pick a word and write a thesaurus entry listing words at all diction levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises broaden lexical choices and increase sensitivity to register; compare your entries to real thesaurus/dictionary entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax transformation exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a passage and transform every sentence so it says approximately the same thing in different syntax; build tight parallels; rewrite non-periodic sentences as periodic ones; rest sentences to emphasize different points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These force awareness of syntactic options and how syntax controls emphasis, information flow, and rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tight parallels and periodic sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct sentences with exact parallel structures and rewrite sentences into periodic form so grammatical and physical ends coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises enhance control of coordination and subordination; practice making periodic sentences for cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical figures (tropes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work through a handbook of rhetorical figures and write an example for each figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generating examples deepens understanding of rhetorical devices; doing them superficially gives limited benefit — producing actual examples gives real practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary 'which' (which vs that rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'which' only where appropriate; unnecessary use of 'which' on paper conveys a bad, nervous tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice that/which contrasts; Don and Mary‑Claire note that misuses appear under pressure. Keep an eye on online copies and edit out 'wicked whiches.' Fowler's rule is referenced; check speech vs writing contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text must make sense without subsection titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your text reads coherently if subsection titles are omitted; do not rely on a subheading as an 'integral' part of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a heading is 'Contour Integration' don't write 'This technique, invented by Cauchy, is used...' where 'this technique' depends on the heading; instead, make the paragraph self-contained: 'The technique of integrating along curves in the complex plane, invented by Cauchy, is used...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms early and for your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Define graph-theory and other technical terms clearly at the start, because different authors may use terms inconsistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what background your readers share and define at the start even basic terms or symbols that may not be universally understood (e.g., path vs simple path; use of '=' historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct — 'less is more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense multi-part or intimidating definitions where possible; avoid verbosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If portions aren't reused ('W2 is used nowhere else'), condense or remove; prefer simpler statements that serve the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in terminology (especially with co-authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same term for the same concept; avoid having co-authors use different names for identical concepts (e.g., 'dominators' vs 'parents').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistency confuses readers; coordinate terminology when collaborating and avoid defining unused terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't define symbols/terms you never use
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid introducing notation or symbols that do not appear in later text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary definitions clutter the paper and distract the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct tense usage for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use present tense for timeless facts (e.g., 'algorithms have' not 'had' when speaking of their worst-case complexities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between timeless statements about objects and time-varying statements about knowledge or problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation style and parenthetical references
rubrics_metrics.description: References should preferably be parenthetical and should not break sentence flow (avoid 'Tarjan[Gab83]' without space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format citations so sentences remain readable when citations are ignored; follow a consistent style and consider automated numbering (TeX/bib systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage guided by speech pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rough guide, put a comma where a speaker would pause to draw breath; avoid too many commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given where commas around a symbol were unnecessary; overpunctuation distorts readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple rules rather than over-optimized ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a simple clear rule instead of an optimal but complex one (e.g., omit extraneous conditions if a simpler statement suffices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical clarity often trumps theoretical optimality in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous word usage and overloaded terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for words used in multiple senses in the same context (e.g., 'left' as direction vs past tense; 'plane' as complex plane vs airplane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose or rename to avoid collisions; make intended meaning explicit to prevent reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct genitive/possessive for symbols and words
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write 'Hi S descendants' — include apostrophes where needed ('Hi's descendants'), and prefer grammatical constructions like 'each Hi is...' to form plurals of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid awkward symbol plurals that create parsing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent bad line breaks with ties in TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ties (nonbreakable spaces) after words when you don't want line breaks to separate them from following words (e.g., after 'dominates', or between 'e' and 'is').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps keep technical phrases intact visually and semantically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence examples so they build on one another
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of examples that build upon each other is more useful than unrelated examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange illustrative examples pedagogically to show progressive structure or generalization (Haddad/Schiiffer paper praised for this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use lemmas/theorems before they are proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid citing a lemma or theorem earlier in the text than when it is proved, to prevent the appearance of circularity or 'pulling a fast one'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make proof structure and ordering explicit so the reader can follow logical dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing and small typographic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with spacing around parentheses and references (e.g., '4.3 (below)' rather than '4.3(below)'); maintain typographic niceties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small spacing issues disrupt reading; follow standard typesetting conventions.
